limitations_and_boundaries: GEARS must be trained on the same cell type or experimental condition for reliable predictions.
Training GEARS using combinatorial perturbation data is essential for accurate prediction of multigene perturbations.
Confounding factors include cell cycle effects, assumed success of gene editing experiments, and heterogeneity in postperturbation distribution.
The incorporation of knowledge graphs limits GEARS's ability to predict outcomes for poorly connected genes in the graph.

research_questions.statement: How can we predict transcriptional outcomes of novel multigene perturbations?

provenance.text_excerpt: GEARS is able to predict outcomes of perturbing combinations consisting of genes that were never experimentally perturbed.

claims.statement: GEARS can predict outcomes of perturbations involving genes never experimentally perturbed before.

provenance.text_excerpt: GEARS improved precision@10 by more than 40% for four of five genetic interaction subtypes

claims.statement: GEARS detects emergent genetic interactions (non-additive) with higher precision than baselines.

provenance.text_excerpt: GEARS exhibited 40% higher precision than existing approaches in predicting four distinct genetic interaction subtypes in a combinatorial perturbation screen and identified the strongest interactions twice as well as prior approaches.

claims.statement: GEARS outperforms existing approaches in predicting transcriptional outcomes of both single and multigene perturbations.

datasets.description: Two genetic perturbation screens: 1,543 perturbations in RPE-1 cells and 1,092 perturbations in K562 cells, each measuring over 170,000 cells using Perturb-seq.
datasets.name: Replogle et al. (2022) Perturb-seq screens

datasets.description: Dataset containing 131 two-gene perturbations, used to evaluate on cases where 0, 1, or 2 genes in the combination are unseen during training.
datasets.name: Norman et al. (2019) combinatorial perturbation screen

evidence_spans.content: GEARS incorporates a gene coexpression knowledge graph and a Gene Ontology-derived knowledge graph.

provenance.text_excerpt: GEARS does this by incorporating prior knowledge of gene–gene relationships using a gene coexpression knowledge graph when learning gene embeddings and a Gene Ontology (GO)-derived knowledge graph when learning gene perturbation embeddings

experiments_or_tasks: Predicting new biologically meaningful phenotypes for all pairwise combinations of 102 genes from Norman et al. dataset.
Predicting non-additive combinatorial perturbation effects (genetic interaction subtypes: synergy, suppression, neomorphism, redundancy, epistasis).
Predicting single-gene perturbation transcriptional responses using GEARS on Replogle et al. datasets (RPE-1 and K562 cells).
Predicting two-gene perturbation outcomes using GEARS on Norman et al. dataset, with three generalization classes (0/2, 1/2, 2/2 unseen).

methods.name: GEARS (Graph-Enhanced Gene Activation and Repression Simulator)
methods.protocol_description: Integrates deep learning with a knowledge graph of gene–gene relationships (gene coexpression and Gene Ontology) to predict transcriptional responses to single and multigene perturbations. Uses distinct gene and perturbation embeddings, a GNN to propagate information on graphs, and a cross-gene MLP layer. Trained using a Bayesian formulation to output uncertainty. Five models trained with different data splits for confidence intervals.

methods.name: CPA (existing deep learning-based model)
methods.protocol_description: An alternative deep learning-based model used as a baseline for comparison.

methods.name: No perturbation baseline
methods.protocol_description: Assumes perturbation results in no change in gene expression.

methods.name: Gene regulatory network (GRN) baseline (adapted from CellOracle)
methods.protocol_description: Infers a gene regulatory network and linearly propagates effects of perturbing a gene along this network.

study_units.name: GEARS model development and evaluation

results.value_raw_text: GEARS improved precision@10 by more than 40% for four of five genetic interaction subtypes, and exceeded 90% for redundancy and epistasis.

results.metric_name: Correlation coefficient (R2) for genetic interaction scores

provenance.text_excerpt: the correlation coefficient (R2) was approximately 0.4 for synergy, neomorphism and redundancy, whereas it was only around 0.0 for the same interactions when predicted by CPA

results.value_raw_text: R2 was approximately 0.4 for synergy, neomorphism and redundancy for GEARS, compared to around 0.0 for CPA.

provenance.text_excerpt: GEARS improves performance by more than 30% across all cases (Fig. 2f), with the highest improvement of 53% observed when both perturbed genes in the combination are unseen.

results.value_raw_text: GEARS improves performance by more than 30% across all generalization cases, with highest improvement of 53% when both genes unseen.

provenance.text_excerpt: GEARS significantly outperformed all baselines on both datasets with an m.s.e. improvement of 30–50%

results.value_raw_text: GEARS improves MSE by 30-50% over baselines on RPE-1 and K562 datasets.
